MATERIA

THE VEGETABLE KINGDOM.

Published by JOH. JAC. PALM
1787.

Not even the forests, nor the more forbidding face of Nature, are without medicines, since that sacred Parent of all things everywhere provides remedies for mankind, so that even the wilderness itself became Medicine. — Here Medicine was born. — Nature alone had seen fit that remedies should be ready for common use, easy to discover, and without cost.

PLINY. Natural History. XXIV. 1.

PREFACE.

There will be no shortage of people who may object that I have perhaps taken on a superfluous labor in collecting the Vegetable Materia Medica of North America. For since, in our more recent age, the stock of medicines has grown into so great and manifold a variety, and the most distinguished men of our time devote every effort to freeing the pharmacies from the burden of superfluous and useless items, while on the other hand new remedies are continually being proposed and praised — many people, with equal frequency and, indeed, with some justice, complain that these are idle and worthless. Lest I therefore incur their harsher judgment, it seems necessary to explain in a few words the purpose and origin of this work. During nearly seven years spent in various parts of North America, I devoted whatever time remained to me and whatever spare hours I could find to the study of botany. Anxious, however, not to spend my time in what might seem an altogether useless curiosity...

iv PREFACE.

I began to record for my own use those American plants whose properties and uses were not yet sufficiently known. I did the same when, after peace was restored, I visited the southern American Provinces, namely Maryland, Virginia and the mountain ranges adjacent to them, both Carolinas, Florida, and the Bahama Islands; everywhere I diligently inquired what plants native to those regions might be turned to medical uses, and whatever plants were pointed out or shown to me by practitioners of medicine, empirics, country folk, and indeed even old women, I recorded them all, and added whatever I could discover about their properties. Thus it came about that I assembled a long catalogue of simples, among which some were entirely new, some known only to a few, while others were already more widely recognized. I could not but marvel at the riches which bountiful Nature has given to the inhabitants of America, and at the remarkable generosity with which she has supplied those regions, far and wide, with all things — or at least with the most necessary aids — for routing a sufficiently powerful army of diseases; yet at the same time I was grieved that so many incomparable indigenous and readily available medicaments were in that very America almost entirely neglected, or familiar only to very few of its inhabitants. For the great majority of men practicing medicine in America, otherwise learned and praiseworthy gentlemen, having been educated either in European schools or in the colleges that exist in America, in the Arts

PREFACE. v

Those who have laid the foundations of the art of healing have nonetheless, following the customary compendiums of European physicians regarding their Materia Medica, been taught; and thus, pursuing a well-worn path, they neglect those things which are commonly used throughout their individual provinces — the domestic simples and remedies — and, as is nearly everywhere the custom, they look with longing toward foreign things in which they abound most. Various reasons must be assigned for this negligence. Some are displeased by the pompous jumble of medicines, and, attaching themselves to a more select and superior apparatus, they spurn all the rest. Others think it beneath the dignity of a physician to employ folk remedies and native medicines. Some are unwilling to leave the beaten path, others do not know how, and not just anyone dares to venture into new territory; for those things are more readily trusted which are put forward by a Master as proven, and which are judged to bear the seal of ancient truth. Above all, however, we must add to the reasons already named the neglect, persisting until now, of the study of natural history and Botany in particular among Americans. For, frightened by the difficulty of this most noble science, it was valued far more cheaply than it deserved — a science which now begins more and more to be cherished. Men of public spirit had not, indeed, failed to see the advantages to be gained from this; those who for many years past have earnestly desired that the qualities and uses of native plants might be more thoroughly investigated.

VI PREFACE.

To obtain the knowledge of botany necessary for this purpose, no one will deny that it is essential, unless one who is content to conduct experiments in a blind manner, or, having gathered them, is entirely indifferent to communicating with others and properly identifying the bodies under discussion. Thus the illustrious LINNAEUS long ago counted among the Obstacles of Medicine the ignorance of physicians and pharmacists in botanical matters, and their neglect of the natural classes and of the Euporistics *). Since, therefore, in collecting medicinal plants of America I had accomplished more than anyone before me, and had acquired a broader knowledge of them, I resolved to take the opportunity, while in America itself, to make a catalog of them available to the public; and in this undertaking I was encouraged by the words and letters of many American friends. Yet to complete this work, while traveling through America, I had neither leisure nor opportunity; for I found myself at the same time deprived of the necessary aids to sustain, as far as was possible, a complete history of the American Materia Medica. I was aware that the illustrious LINNAEUS had long since made public observations on the properties and uses of various North American plants, recorded by BARTRAM **); and that CLAYTONIUS, in the Flora Virginica, and COLDENIVM, in the Flora

PREFACE. VII

Of New York, Kalm in his itinerary, Catesby in his history of the Plants of Carolina, and an anonymous writer on the Plants of Georgia — to say nothing of others — I believed it would be worthwhile to bring together their observations and annotations and to add my own, so that I might present at once all the knowledge of the powers and uses of American plants that can be gathered from both the living and the dead.

I venture to hope that these pages will be pleasing both to those practicing Medicine in America and to American citizens generally, and likewise that they will prove useful in some measure to European physicians. We certainly owe much to those regions of the western world, and noble remedies of both Americas are well known to us — indeed so familiar and commonplace that perhaps no European physician would wish to be without them. Yet knowledge of these things continually stirred a desire to learn more and raised ever greater expectations, so that whatever was brought from that part of the world was always received with open hands. European physicians and students of Natural Science will find this volume welcome, presenting at a single glance all the medicinal substances of the vast regions of North America that have come to light up to the present time. VIII PREFACE.

I still do not have a complete knowledge of the internal parts; nor will I deny that the knowledge of some has escaped me. Although this acquaintance with the simple plants of remote lands does not appear to promise an absolute benefit or utility to European physicians, it may suffice at least to have contributed to a general knowledge of herbs created for the benefit of mankind. But if an unjust critic were to reproach me for merely naming those plants of which the distinguished men mentioned above made no mention, and which I added as new, it will then be evident that I have satisfied neither one party nor the other satisfactorily. For the nature of the undertaking required that the names, qualities, and powers even of those plants which are already known to us in Europe with the utmost precision, should be set down again verbatim. Yet in terms briefer and more concise than those found in the illustrious Linnaeus's Materia Medica — something that could scarcely be achieved with his words — and so, rather than transcribing those complete titles here, the insult of a foolish plagiarist does not attach to me. Since the principle of brevity as well as clarity had to be observed, I decided to follow the Linnaean method throughout the rest as well; and for this reason, with entries separated by lines, I have indicated the Specific Name, Synonyms, Native Localities, Pharmacopoeial Name, Qualities, Powers, and Uses.

What I have received, and of what nature, I report back. I was wholly unable to verify the truth of the assertions by personal trial or observation. Nor will I deny that among the plants listed there may be some whose uses fall short of expec-

satisfy the promise and expectation less; yet I do not doubt that the great praise spoken of it will be sustained in its effect. I therefore wish to commend, again and again, the further investigation of this matter to American physicians, for whom the opportunity is given, and who ought to have at heart both the benefit of Medicine and of their Homeland: being absent in the meantime, I believed I would be of service to posterity; by enumerating the herbs whose virtue has been praised; by demonstrating that what was once found to be useful should not fall into oblivion; by spreading knowledge of domestic medicines, easily prepared by common means and without expense; by directing the attention of Americans toward their own native resources; and by showing, finally, how much it matters for Physicians to know their indigenous plants well. For Americans will see, from this vast catalog of their own simples, that if they wished, they could easily do without foreign medicines, if not all, at least the great majority. For the lands of those regions produce and bring forth so many and such varied plants, suited to the nature of their situation and soil, that whatever remedies are needed for the practice of rational medicine can, with very few exceptions, be obtained from their own territory. For the geographical situation of those regions, extending from the farthest North toward the South across the continent of North America, more than any other place, unites all climates and the plants of all climates. This natural conjunction profits still further from the fact that the Colonies facing East, as it were,

x PREFACE.

born of one blood, they may use the same language, laws, and customs, whereby the mutual commerce of goods and letters is altogether facilitated, and one is encouraged to hope for the most fruitful exchange of studies, inventions, and discoveries.

Besides the plants of America enumerated here, many will perhaps find that, unless all indications are sufficient, certain exotic ones are necessary to resolve all the numbers. But there are few. South America and the neighboring West Indian Islands will therefore provide:

Cinchona bark, Ipecacuanha root,
Vanilla, Ginger root, Costus dulcis,
Black and long Pepper, Cinnamon.

From the East Indies and other places are to be sought:

Camphor, Cloves, Cinnamon,
Benzoin,
Copaiba, Musk, Myrrh, Ammoniac gum.

Certain other things are drawn from Europe, on account of the convenience of trade, up to the present time. But there are among these things which, truly necessary for Americans, and which in the future may be cultivated abundantly and at little cost in the gardens of America itself, since the variety of sky and soil excludes nothing. Such are:

American physicians should therefore take upon themselves the further investigation of these plants, but with the care to observe diligently what they apply and with what success. By experimenting with new remedies in this way, it is worth noting that the properties of these same plants may be heightened or diminished as they grow in warmer or colder climates, as we have found to be the case with various American plants; repeated experiments must therefore be established in different regions before judgment is passed on the reputed virtues of any given plant.

The Bahama Islands, strictly speaking, do not belong to North America; yet since they supply various and rather excellent medicinal substances, I thought it not unreasonable that these should be included; for this will be excused by their proximity, and by the constant commerce between those islands and the mainland, and further by the similarity of climates and of natural resources, which

PREFACE. xv

than the more southerly parts of Florida have with those islands. For the peninsula of Florida extends to 25 degrees of latitude, and very many of the Bahama Islands lie under the same, and even higher, latitude. It is also worth noting that the North American continent, according to geographical division, includes also that Isthmus and the Gulf of Mexico between it and the Pacific Ocean, namely the Province of Mexico and others; so that accordingly, if one had chosen to take the matter in a broader sense, many more plants which the Torrid Zone produces could have been inserted into our catalogue. But wishing to avoid excessive prolixity, I restricted myself to those regions through which I myself had for the most part traveled.

I collected the common English names of plants with all care, so that those too might find them useful who have an aversion to botany; but they are so varied and inconsistent in different regions, and so often the same names are applied to different plants, and the same plants often have very different names. For some plants I received only trivial names, and endeavored with all effort to work out the systematic name so that it might be established with greater certainty; and in this labor the illustrious SCHREBER assisted me most greatly, whose benevolence, for which he always showed me the greatest favor and for which I always held him in veneration, I make due and grateful mention.

xvi PREFACE.

From the medicines reviewed, dire necessity revealed certain cases — sometimes drawing Europeans traveling to America to make use of them by analogy with familiar remedies. Yet several of the most noteworthy are owed to the Native peoples of America, who either voluntarily or through friendship or for a price disclosed them to European colonists. Moreover, it is believed throughout nearly all of America that many more extraordinary specifics for various diseases are known and familiar to the same Native Americans — the revelation of which, however, they are said to avoid with every effort. Yet I do not know on what grounds. For very few, if any, of their remedies deserve to be honored with the name of specifics; they respond to particular indications, so that, for example, their antisyphilitic remedies are for the most part diuretic, sudorific, or drastically purgative. They practice a purely empirical medicine, now with entirely desirable and wonderful effect, now with quite the opposite result — the various and obvious reasons for which, drawn from consideration of their constitution, habits, way of life, diet, and the size of their doses, are easy to see, and this is not the place to elaborate further. In general, however, no one can maintain that they are more fortunate than we are in treating various diseases, though some have persuaded themselves of this. Against the bite of the Crotalus, or rattlesnake, so many herbs so very different in their qualities are recommended, that we must rightly regard the credibility and efficacy of most of them with suspicion, and this all the more so

PREFACE. XVII

all the more so, since experience has made it sufficiently clear that the lethality or malignancy of such wounds varies enormously according to differences of region, season, the parts wounded, and many other causes, so that no harm sometimes results even when medical treatment is entirely neglected; yet on the other hand it cannot be denied that these same plants offer, in their medicinal qualities, benefits altogether worthy of further investigation; and therefore I wished to omit none of them.

I have recorded only the more certain native localities of the plants, yet the greater number of them, or indeed all or most, are at least shared by a Province in common; where only a single province is thus noted, it is not thereby denied that the same plant occurs in other places as well; and as for those which I have said inhabit provinces that are widely separated — for example, Canada and Virginia, or Pennsylvania and Carolina — it is easily understood that they occur likewise in all the intervening provinces.

What is given in the place of an appendix by way of nomenclature consists of simple substances to be sought from the animal and mineral kingdoms of America, both obsolete and currently in use, and commonly reviewed in medicinal literature. Let Americans take note that their own Homeland provides them with a nearly sufficient supply of these, even though the wealth of these kingdoms is divided
